data.text: Rendering is the most challenging part of generating immersive experiences from the point of view of the system. The 3D graphics pipeline has five stages, the first four being object representation, modeling, lighting, and viewing transformation. After viewing transformation, the view pipeline includes clipping, hidden surface removal, projection transformation, and window-to-viewport transformation. The fifth stage is scan conversion, which transforms a device coordinate description into a screen coordinate description on the pixel grid.
points: Rendering is the most challenging part of generating immersive experiences from the point of view of the system.
The 3D graphics pipeline has five stages, the first four being object representation, modeling, lighting, and viewing transformation.
After the viewing transformation, the view pipeline includes clipping, hidden surface removal, projection transformation, and window-to-viewport transformation.
The fifth stage is scan conversion, which transforms a device coordinate description into a screen coordinate description on the pixel grid.

data.text: The device coordinate system used to define the 2D viewport is continuous, but display devices use a pixel grid where points can only have integer coordinates. Scan conversion, also called rendering or rasterization, is the fifth stage of the process. It uses mapping algorithms to transform continuous viewport coordinates into a discrete pixel-grid coordinate system by choosing the nearest integer-coordinate pixels.
points: The device coordinate system for the 2D viewport is a continuous coordinate system.
A display device uses a pixel grid where points can only have integer coordinates.
Scan conversion maps continuous viewport coordinates into a discrete pixel-grid coordinate system.

data.text: While point rendering uses rounding, naive line-rendering is slow because it requires many floating-point operations. The basic idea for rendering a shape is to map it to a set of pixels as fast as possible by reducing floating-point operations. Bresenham's line-drawing algorithm achieves this by using integer arithmetic to avoid slow operations like rounding and division, which is necessary for interactive graphics like virtual reality.
points: Point rendering uses rounding, but naive line-rendering is slow because it requires many floating-point operations.
The basic idea for rendering a shape is to map it to a set of pixels as fast as possible by reducing floating-point operations.
Bresenham's line-drawing algorithm identifies pixels for a line without using floating-point operations.
Bresenham's algorithm is efficient because it uses integer arithmetic to avoid slow operations like rounding and division.
Efficient line-rendering is necessary for interactive graphics like virtual reality, where a system may need to redraw hundreds of thousands of lines.

data.text: Aliasing is distortion caused by scan conversion when pixels do not exactly match original shapes, which can lead to visible distortion and reduced quality of experience. Anti-aliasing uses complex algorithms to reduce this distortion but adds to the overall computation. Because realistic dynamic content manifoldly increases rendering complexity in VR, the challenge is handling these processes without the user perceiving lag or distortion.
points: Aliasing is distortion caused by scan conversion when pixels do not exactly match original shapes.
Unaddressed aliasing can lead to visible distortion and reduce the quality of experience.
Anti-aliasing uses complex algorithms to reduce distortion but adds to the overall computation.
Realistic dynamic content in VR manifoldly increases rendering complexity.
The challenge is to handle this complexity without the user perceiving lag or distortion.

data.text: A computer graphics programmer does not always need to implement the stages of a graphics pipeline from scratch; instead, the programmer can use graphics libraries and their APIs to deal with lower-level tasks. These APIs are predefined sets of functions that perform specific tasks when invoked with appropriate arguments or parameters. By using these APIs, a programmer eliminates the need to know every detail of the underlying system or platform in order to build a graphics application.
points: Programmers do not always need to implement a graphics pipeline from scratch because they can use graphics libraries and their APIs to handle lower-level tasks.
APIs are predefined sets of functions that perform specific tasks when invoked with appropriate arguments or parameters.
APIs eliminate the need for a programmer to know every detail of the underlying system or platform to build a graphics application.

data.text: A layered VR software architecture connects applications to hardware through intermediate layers like SDKs, engines, and rendering libraries. Developers rely on the SDK to access the VR engine, which allows them to handle graphics through rendering library APIs without directly accessing those libraries.
points: VR software architecture consists of several layers between the application and the hardware.
Developers use the SDK and VR engine to manage graphics without directly accessing native rendering libraries.

data.text: GPUs are multicore systems that exploit parallelism to perform simple arithmetic simultaneously. They process triangular meshes by transforming vertices and computing vertex colors simultaneously, then calculate the colors of overlapped pixels in parallel during rasterization. Finally, the GPU performs surface texturing and hidden surface removal to complete pixel processing.
points: GPUs are multicore systems that exploit parallelism to perform simple arithmetic simultaneously.
The GPU processes triangular meshes by transforming vertices and computing vertex colors simultaneously.
Rasterization determines which pixels are overlapped by triangles and calculates their colors in parallel.
The GPU finishes pixel processing by performing surface texturing and hidden surface removal.
